The Commonwealth of Massachusetts
Executive Office of Environmental Affairs
Department of Environmental Quality Engineering
100 Cambridge Street
Boston, Massachusetts 02202
Comments of the
DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ENGINEERING
on the Draft EIS,
CITY OF BOSTON
Clearance of Unsafe Buildings
There are a number of points in this draft statement that require correction, amplification, or modification. Observation on these points will be divided into the subsections on air quality, water quality, and solid waste. In general, whenever the Department of Public Health, Division of Environmental Health, is mentioned, it should be replaced by the Department of Environmental Quality Engineering (D.E.Q.E.).
Air Quality: This section is particularly deficient, adopting an extremely simplistic approach to a complex problem. Basic assumptions are incorrect or inadequate and lead to conclusions that cannot be justified with the data made available.
Air quality standards for particulates are determined for total suspended particulates, not just for the smaller respirable sizes, whether at a given cut-off point like 10 microns or for any particular range of sizes. The real measurement is for those particulates which effectively become airborne and suspended. The on-site monitoring was apparently carried out at street level and, as stated, at very close range, both conditions being inappropriate for obtaining accurate readings.
The methodology for converting total suspended particulates into projected 24-hour averages is not specified. In discussing the impact of demolition on air quality it appears that consultants are unaware that there exist 24-hour standards for both primary and secondary standards. Considerations of impact increased TSP on yearly averages in Boston sites has been ignored.
It is not clear as to how the calculations were made which converted menitored dust into total amount of dust (and particulates) produced. The appropriate linkages and assumptions are not available for examination and critique. Calculations or assumptions for total Boston dust fall are missing. The added impact from some demolition firms working very long hours is apparently not considered. In carrying out analysis of effectiveness of controls, effects of intermittent controls were not measured, but only assumed.
